summary: A status report on parameters, meaning numbers and keywords, used in protocols in the Internet community. It replaces RFC 1010, is historic, was updated by RFC 1349, and was replaced by RFC 1340.

plainLanguage.summary:
Two programs can only understand each other if they agree on what each number means. This RFC is the list of those agreements for the Internet: which protocol number is UDP, which port number is mail, which hardware type code is Ethernet.

It is a status report rather than a protocol. It was issued quarterly, and it has since been replaced by RFC 1340.

what are the arp operation codes
what is an assigned numbers rfc
subtitle: The quarterly status report of the numbers and keywords used in Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Protocols are only interoperable if everyone agrees on which number means what, and the set of agreed numbers grows as new protocols are defined.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1060 lists the assigned values for a long series of registries: IP version and protocol numbers, port numbers, multicast addresses, hardware type codes, option numbers and a set of name lists. Each entry names the value, its keyword and the document that assigned it.
tldr.outcome: The document was issued quarterly and has since been obsoleted by RFC 1340 and updated by RFC 1349. It points readers to IANA for current values.

sections.title: Purpose, Scope and Notation
sections.content:
RFC 1060 is a status report on the parameters, meaning numbers and keywords, used in protocols in the Internet community. It records the values currently assigned from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. The document was to be updated periodically, and it says that current information can be obtained from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). Anyone developing a protocol or application that needs a link, socket or port number is told to contact IANA to get an assignment.

Most of the protocols listed are documented in the RFC series, but some of the items are undocumented. The RFC also notes that the Internet Activities Board publishes the IAB Official Protocol Standards, which describes the state of standardization of the protocols in use.

The document sets out the conventions used throughout. Numbers are written in decimal, and data is shown in big-endian order: fields are described from left to right, with the most significant octet on the left. Where a diagram shows a group of octets, they are transmitted in the order they are numbered. When an octet stands for a numeric quantity, the leftmost bit is the most significant one, so the diagram 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 represents the value 170.

The first registry in the document is a summary of special IP addresses. There are five classes of IP address, A through E, and Class D and Class E are reserved for experimental use. A gateway not taking part in those experiments must ignore all datagrams with a Class D or Class E destination address, and no ICMP Destination Unreachable or ICMP Redirect message may result from receiving such a datagram. The document then lists the special cases: {0, 0} for this host on this network, {-1, -1} for the limited broadcast, {127, any} for the internal host loopback address, and directed broadcasts for a network or a subnet.
sections.plainLanguage:
The RFC records the agreed meaning of every number the Internet uses, and it explains the notation the rest of the document uses.

One rule stands out: a gateway must ignore datagrams addressed to the experimental address classes, and must not answer them with an error message.

sections.title: Version, Protocol and Port Numbers
sections.content:
The IP header carries a 4-bit field naming the version of the Internet protocol. Version 4 is assigned to the Internet Protocol, version 5 to ST Datagram Mode, and versions 0 and 15 are reserved. The IP header also carries an 8-bit field called Protocol, which names the next-level protocol. The registry assigns 1 to ICMP, 2 to IGMP, 6 to TCP, 8 to the Exterior Gateway Protocol, 17 to UDP and 41 to IPv6 among the values in use, with ranges left unassigned and some slots reserved for private use.

Ports are used in TCP to name the ends of logical connections that carry long-term conversations. For the purpose of serving callers that are not already known, a service contact port is defined for each service, sometimes called the well-known port. The same assignments are used, as far as possible, with UDP and with ISO-TP4. The assigned ports use a small part of the possible port numbers: all except the low-order eight bits are cleared to zero, and the low-order eight bits are what the table lists. The table gives 25 to Simple Mail Transfer, 21 to the FTP control connection and 20 to FTP data, 23 to Telnet, 69 to TFTP, 53 to the Domain Name Server and 43 to the Who Is service, among many others.

A separate section lists UNIX ports, and the document closes with large tables of machine names, system names, protocol and service names and terminal type names. A protocol or service name may be up to 40 characters of uppercase letters, digits and the hyphen, must start with a letter and must end with a letter or a digit. Machine names may also use the slash, and system names may use both the hyphen and the slash.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Protocol header has a field for the protocol number, and the first protocol number 1 is ICMP, number 6 is TCP and number 17 is UDP. The port table says which numbers services listen on, such as 25 for mail and 23 for Telnet.

sections.title: Multicast and Hardware Addresses
sections.content:
The multicast section lists the addresses reserved for IP multicast groups, following the host extensions for IP multicasting in RFC 1112. Among them are 224.0.0.0, reserved, 224.0.0.1 for all hosts on this subnet, 224.0.0.4 for DVMRP routers and 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for OSPF routers and designated routers. When multicast is used on an Ethernet or IEEE 802 network, the 23 low-order bits of the IP multicast address are placed in the low-order 23 bits of the Ethernet multicast address.

For that to work, IANA owns a block of Ethernet addresses, given in IEEE binary as 0000 0000 0000 0000 0111 1010, which in dotted decimal is 0.0.94. In the memory representation that most programmers deal with, the block runs from 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF in hex, or from 1.0.94.0.0.0 to 1.0.94.127.255.255 in dotted decimal. The first bit of the block marks an Ethernet multicast address, and the next bit says whether the address is an Internet multicast address or one assigned by IANA for other uses.

The document also lists the Ethernet type numbers of interest, where 2048 is the DoD IP type and 2054 is ARP, the Ethernet vendor address components that let an organisation be identified from the first three octets of its address, and the Ethernet multicast addresses.

Two small registries complete the address material. The Address Resolution Protocol has operation codes 1 for a request and 2 for a reply, and hardware type codes that run from 1 for Ethernet to 12 for LocalNet. The Reverse Address Resolution Protocol has operation codes 3 and 4 for reverse request and reverse reply, and the Dynamic Reverse ARP extension adds 5, 6 and 7 for its request, reply and error.
sections.plainLanguage: When one host sends to a group of hosts, it uses a multicast address. The RFC lists the group addresses and the block of Ethernet addresses that carry them, and it lists the small sets of codes used by ARP and RARP.

sections.title: TOS, TTL and Protocol Option Registries
sections.content:
The IP Type of Service field carries three binary attributes: low delay, high throughput and high reliability. An attribute bit is turned on to mean better. The three cannot all be optimised at once, and the algorithms discussed tend to make better values mutually exclusive, so the recommended values have at most one bit on. Protocols that interact directly with a person should choose low delay, transfers of large blocks of data need high throughput, and datagram-based network management functions care most about high reliability.

The recommended values are then tabulated per protocol. Telnet, TFTP, the FTP control connection, the SMTP command phase and a UDP domain name query all take low delay; the FTP data connection, the SMTP data phase and a domain zone transfer take high throughput; any interior gateway protocol and SNMP take high reliability; and NNTP, ICMP errors, ICMP queries, EGP and BOOTP take none of the three. An application not listed is told to choose low delay (1 0 0) or high throughput (0 1 0). If an implementation cannot change the Type of Service during a connection, the recommended value on opening the connection is (0,0,0).

The recommended default TTL for IP is 32. The domain system registry lists the CLASS parameter, with 1 for Internet and 65535 reserved. The BOOTP section lists the vendor information extensions, where tag 1 is the subnet mask, 2 the time zone, 3 the gateways, 12 the hostname and 13 the boot file size, and 255 ends the list.

Two further registries cover protocol options. The Telnet option list numbers 0 for binary transmission, 1 for echo, 3 for suppress go ahead, 24 for terminal type, 34 for linemode and 255 for the extended options list. The mail encryption types section records that RFC 822 allows encryption types to be assigned but that none have been, and points at the Mail Privacy procedures instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The Type of Service field has three switches: low delay, high throughput and high reliability. The RFC says which one to set for each common protocol, and gives the recommended default time to live of 32.

sections.title: Registries for Other Networks and Protocols
sections.content:
A large part of the document records numbers that belong to networks other than the Internet. There are registries for ARPANET and MILNET logical addresses, ARPANET and MILNET link numbers, and the mapping between ARPANET and MILNET numbers and X.25 addresses. There are the IEEE 802 numbers of interest, the XNS protocol types, the PRONET 80 type numbers, and the X.25 type numbers defined by CCITT for the high-order two bits of the first octet of call user data. There is also a registry of public data network numbers, which maps Internet addresses to X.121 addresses for the international system of public data networks.

The protocol and type field section gives two tables showing how a datagram of one kind can be carried in a datagram of another kind, for example sending an Internet datagram over 10 Mb Ethernet or sending an NS datagram over the ARPANET. The Ethernet type for DoD IP is 1001 in octal on 3 Mb Ethernet and 0800 in hex on 10 Mb Ethernet, and the ARPANET link number for DoD IP is 155 in decimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the numbers in the RFC belong to older networks, such as the ARPANET and X.25, and some describe how one network's packets are carried inside another's. The RFC lists them so that the gateways and hosts that interconnect these networks agree on the values.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of RFC 1060 says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document is a status report on assigned values rather than a protocol specification, so it defines no behaviour that could be attacked.

The one place where the document does carry a rule is the list of special IP addresses, where it states that a gateway which is not taking part in the Class D and Class E experiments must ignore all datagrams with such a destination address, and that no ICMP Destination Unreachable or ICMP Redirect message must result from receiving them.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC has almost nothing to say about security. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed, because the document assigns numbers rather than describing behaviour.
